[a3:v1000022:r1000105:block:1003856:1:0]
Aerial manipulation is gaining popularity due to its ability to operate freely in 3D space, particularly in high-altitude environments that are difficult for humans to access [2]–[4]. Although fully autonomous manipulation remains the ultimate goal for robotics researchers, the complexity of the aerial environment necessitates keeping a human operator in the loop [5]. In our previous work [1], we proposed a six-degree-of-freedom teleoperation framework for aerial manipulation. Specifically, we designed four interaction modes for different tasks, including Spherical Mode and Cartesian Mode for long-range movement, Operation Mode for precise manipulation, and Locking Mode for temporary pauses, where hand gestures were utilized for seamless mode switching. The proposed framework was evaluated through a valve-turning task1, and to the best of our knowledge, this was the first time the rotational dexterity of the human wrist was intuitively demonstrated on an omnidirectional aerial robot. However, due to the limitations of both the controller and the physical structure of human forearm, we were not able to achieve continuous rotation.

[a3:v1000025:r1000108:block:1003996:1:0]
Developing algorithms enabling robot prehensile manipulation tasks in dynamic real-world environments remains a major challenge in robotics. The manipulation problem aims at finding a set of suitable robot controls to change the state of an object from an initial to a desired configuration. More specifically, prehensile manipulation involves keeping the object grasped while the whole robot executes the manipulation using its control system [1]. For example opening a fridge is prehensile manipulating switching the object state from closed to open by grasping the fridge hammer during the whole robot motion. Solving robotic prehensile manipulation problems is inherently difficult due to the sparse nature of the grasping problem. In such scenarios, the space of solutions is extremely large, yet successful feedback is rare, making learning-based approaches particularly challenging. Moreover, the environments in which robots operate are highly variable—each static scene can differ significantly in object positions, shapes, levels of clutter, and semantic context [2]. For these reasons, prehensile manipulation is often described as an open-world or open-ended problem.

Heading: Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation > Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation > I. INTRODUCTION

### [a3:v1000022:r1000105:block:1003856:1:0]

Aerial manipulation is gaining popularity due to its ability to operate freely in 3D space, particularly in high-altitude environments that are difficult for humans to access [2]–[4]. Although fully autonomous manipulation remains the ultimate goal for robotics researchers, the complexity of the aerial environment necessitates keeping a human operator in the loop [5]. In our previous work [1], we proposed a six-degree-of-freedom teleoperation framework for aerial manipulation. Specifically, we designed four interaction modes for different tasks, including Spherical Mode and Cartesian Mode for long-range movement, Operation Mode for precise manipulation, and Locking Mode for temporary pauses, where hand gestures were utilized for seamless mode switching. The proposed framework was evaluated through a valve-turning task1, and to the best of our knowledge, this was the first time the rotational dexterity of the human wrist was intuitively demonstrated on an omnidirectional aerial robot. However, due to the limitations of both the controller and the physical structure of human forearm, we were not able to achieve continuous rotation.

## Source scope 5 | Document/version 3: ARXIV180-2efec0b0b2f728dd1db75073 — Towards Robust Prehensile Manipulation in Open-Ended Environments
Heading: Towards Robust Prehensile Manipulation in Open-Ended Environments > Towards Robust Prehensile Manipulation in Open-Ended Environments > 1. INTRODUCTION TO PREHENSILE MANIPULATION

### [a3:v1000025:r1000108:block:1003996:1:0]

Developing algorithms enabling robot prehensile manipulation tasks in dynamic real-world environments remains a major challenge in robotics. The manipulation problem aims at finding a set of suitable robot controls to change the state of an object from an initial to a desired configuration. More specifically, prehensile manipulation involves keeping the object grasped while the whole robot executes the manipulation using its control system [1]. For example opening a fridge is prehensile manipulating switching the object state from closed to open by grasping the fridge hammer during the whole robot motion. Solving robotic prehensile manipulation problems is inherently difficult due to the sparse nature of the grasping problem. In such scenarios, the space of solutions is extremely large, yet successful feedback is rare, making learning-based approaches particularly challenging. Moreover, the environments in which robots operate are highly variable—each static scene can differ significantly in object positions, shapes, levels of clutter, and semantic context [2]. For these reasons, prehensile manipulation is often described as an open-world or open-ended problem.

On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > I. INTRODUCTION > A. Related Work
Imaging Spectroscopy data consists of many spectrally narrow bands, sensors considered in this work span between 380 to 2500nm. As such, they offer visibility of a number of trace gases, nonetheless robust detection of these events remains challenging. The work of [3] first proposes the approach of using ML models for on-board detection of methane leak events. It defines two ways of processing data, either using end-to-end ML models which process radiance data directly, or via dependence on MF products. The work of [4] follows up in the direction of speeding up MF computations and then using ML models to reduce the number of false alarms.

[a3:v1000188:r1000277:block:1011699:1:0]
On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > IV. CONCLUSION
We present initial results from the deployment of machine learning models on-board of aerial platform used in the Tokyo-FC campaign. We present what we believe to be the first automated detection of methane leak on-board with machine learning, a significant and logical next step to the work of [1]. Predictions of our model, alongside with the collected data are available in the public portal at3. As future research, we aim to explore the usage of machine learning models recently proposed in [2] for multi-species detection of trace gases.

[a3:v1000188:r1000277:block:1011687:1:0]
On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > II. METHODOLOGY > B. Proxy environment
We start with the full EMIT on-the-ground pipeline described in [5]. First, we skip several steps in order to speed up the processing, while observing minimal differences in the computed products. In all cases, we avoid the order sorting filter (OSF) correction, as it affects bands outside of typical methane visibility (2100-2500nm). We also explore skipping bad pixel and ghost correction. We vectorise computations and merge repeated operations where possible. We highlight that the full on-the-ground pipeline strives for accurate science ready data products, meanwhile for fast on-board detection of very large methane leak events, some shortcuts can be taken. As a second optional step, we compute the matched filter product. We use a non-iterative spectrally wide variant. Finally, in the third step, we use a machine learning model either on the radiance data, or on the matched filter product computed for the same location. For end-to-end radiance data processing, we leverage models published in [3], namely the HyperEfficientViT (ConvUp) variant. Imaging Spectroscopy data consists of many spectrally narrow bands, sensors considered in this work span between 380 to 2500nm. As such, they offer visibility of a number of trace gases, nonetheless robust detection of these events remains challenging. The work of [3] first proposes the approach of using ML models for on-board detection of methane leak events. It defines two ways of processing data, either using end-to-end ML models which process radiance data directly, or via dependence on MF products. The work of [4] follows up in the direction of speeding up MF computations and then using ML models to reduce the number of false alarms.

We present initial results from the deployment of machine learning models on-board of aerial platform used in the Tokyo-FC campaign. We present what we believe to be the first automated detection of methane leak on-board with machine learning, a significant and logical next step to the work of [1]. Predictions of our model, alongside with the collected data are available in the public portal at3. As future research, we aim to explore the usage of machine learning models recently proposed in [2] for multi-species detection of trace gases.

On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > II. METHODOLOGY > B. Proxy environment
We start with the full EMIT on-the-ground pipeline described in [5]. First, we skip several steps in order to speed up the processing, while observing minimal differences in the computed products. In all cases, we avoid the order sorting filter (OSF) correction, as it affects bands outside of typical methane visibility (2100-2500nm). We also explore skipping bad pixel and ghost correction. We vectorise computations and merge repeated operations where possible. We highlight that the full on-the-ground pipeline strives for accurate science ready data products, meanwhile for fast on-board detection of very large methane leak events, some shortcuts can be taken. As a second optional step, we compute the matched filter product. We use a non-iterative spectrally wide variant. Finally, in the third step, we use a machine learning model either on the radiance data, or on the matched filter product computed for the same location. For end-to-end radiance data processing, we leverage models published in [3], namely the HyperEfficientViT (ConvUp) variant. For matched filter dependent models, we use models released in [6] using the U-Net architecture.

Abstract—Omics data analysis is crucial for studying complex diseases, but its high dimensionality and heterogeneity challenge classical statistical and machine learning methods. Graph neural networks have emerged as promising alternatives, yet the optimal strategies for their design and optimization in real-world biomedical challenges remain unclear. This study evaluates various graph representation learning models for case-control classification using high-throughput biological data from Parkinson's disease and control samples. We compare topologies derived from sample similarity networks and molecular interaction networks, including protein-protein and metabolite-metabolite interactions (PPI, MMI). Graph Convolutional Network (GCNs), Chebyshev spectral graph convolution (ChebyNet), and Graph Attention Network (GAT), are evaluated alongside advanced architectures like graph transformers, the graph U-net, and simpler models like multilayer perceptron (MLP).

### [a3:v1000000:r1000023:block:1001491:1:0]

Digital Twin Software simulates DENSO robots and equipment within a 3D virtual environment. It integrates the "realvirtual.io" software, which is designed for building digital twin spaces, with "Unity," the world's leading 3D development platform. It can help improve and optimize processes, such as verifying layouts without purchasing any actual equipment, training workers, and reducing setup adjustment time.

Unity is the world's most popular platform for 3D development. In addition to its use in game development, Unity now provides the "Unity Industry" application for industrial purposes. As a game creation platform, it is highly effective for building digital twin environments, utilizing advanced 3D technologies and physics.

--- End source scope ---

Heading: TEST A3 DigitalTwinSoftware > Digital Twin Software > Overview of digital twin component software > ● realvirtual.io-Professional

### [a3:v1000020:r1000086:block:1003767:1:0]

Realvirtual.io Professional is a Unity add-on that simplifies the creation of equipment design simulations. With its extensive library of assets, including conveyors and motors, you can intuitively build digital twin environments. It also enables easy simulation of equipment with support for TwinCAT and OPC UA interfaces, PLC connections, and software wiring.

Abstract—Omics data analysis is crucial for studying complex diseases, but its high dimensionality and heterogeneity challenge classical statistical and machine learning methods. Graph neural networks have emerged as promising alternatives, yet the optimal strategies for their design and optimization in real-world biomedical challenges remain unclear. This study evaluates various graph representation learning models for case-control classification using high-throughput biological data from Parkinson's disease and control samples. We compare topologies derived from sample similarity networks and molecular interaction networks, including protein-protein and metabolite-metabolite interactions (PPI, MMI). Graph Convolutional Network (GCNs), Chebyshev spectral graph convolution (ChebyNet), and Graph Attention Network (GAT), are evaluated alongside advanced architectures like graph transformers, the graph U-net, and simpler models like multilayer perceptron (MLP).

Khi thấy các bu-lông của máy nén bị dính dầu, bảng chẩn đoán nêu vị trí rò gas và biện pháp gì?

[a3:v1000188:r1000277:block:1011679:1:0]
Imaging Spectroscopy data consists of many spectrally narrow bands, sensors considered in this work span between 380 to 2500nm. As such, they offer visibility of a number of trace gases, nonetheless robust detection of these events remains challenging. The work of [3] first proposes the approach of using ML models for on-board detection of methane leak events. It defines two ways of processing data, either using end-to-end ML models which process radiance data directly, or via dependence on MF products. The work of [4] follows up in the direction of speeding up MF computations and then using ML models to reduce the number of false alarms.

[a3:v1000188:r1000277:block:1011699:1:0]
We present initial results from the deployment of machine learning models on-board of aerial platform used in the Tokyo-FC campaign. We present what we believe to be the first automated detection of methane leak on-board with machine learning, a significant and logical next step to the work of [1]. Predictions of our model, alongside with the collected data are available in the public portal at3. As future research, we aim to explore the usage of machine learning models recently proposed in [2] for multi-species detection of trace gases.

[a3:v1000188:r1000277:block:1011687:1:0]
We start with the full EMIT on-the-ground pipeline described in [5]. First, we skip several steps in order to speed up the processing, while observing minimal differences in the computed products. In all cases, we avoid the order sorting filter (OSF) correction, as it affects bands outside of typical methane visibility (2100-2500nm). We also explore skipping bad pixel and ghost correction. We vectorise computations and merge repeated operations where possible. We highlight that the full on-the-ground pipeline strives for accurate science ready data products, meanwhile for fast on-board detection of very large methane leak events, some shortcuts can be taken. As a second optional step, we compute the matched filter product. We use a non-iterative spectrally wide variant. Finally, in the third step, we use a machine learning model either on the radiance data, or on the matched filter product computed for the same location. For end-to-end radiance data processing, we leverage models published in [3], namely the HyperEfficientViT (ConvUp) variant. For matched filter dependent models, we use models released in [6] using the U-Net architecture.

### [a3:v1000188:r1000277:block:1011679:1:0]

Imaging Spectroscopy data consists of many spectrally narrow bands, sensors considered in this work span between 380 to 2500nm. As such, they offer visibility of a number of trace gases, nonetheless robust detection of these events remains challenging. The work of [3] first proposes the approach of using ML models for on-board detection of methane leak events. It defines two ways of processing data, either using end-to-end ML models which process radiance data directly, or via dependence on MF products. The work of [4] follows up in the direction of speeding up MF computations and then using ML models to reduce the number of false alarms.

--- End source scope ---

Heading: On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > IV. CONCLUSION

### [a3:v1000188:r1000277:block:1011699:1:0]

We present initial results from the deployment of machine learning models on-board of aerial platform used in the Tokyo-FC campaign. We present what we believe to be the first automated detection of methane leak on-board with machine learning, a significant and logical next step to the work of [1]. Predictions of our model, alongside with the collected data are available in the public portal at3. As future research, we aim to explore the usage of machine learning models recently proposed in [2] for multi-species detection of trace gases.

## Source scope 4 | Document/version 1: ARXIV180-0dff05775f9fe90e11584c73 — On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data
Heading: On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data > II. METHODOLOGY > B. Proxy environment

### [a3:v1000188:r1000277:block:1011687:1:0]

We start with the full EMIT on-the-ground pipeline described in [5]. First, we skip several steps in order to speed up the processing, while observing minimal differences in the computed products. In all cases, we avoid the order sorting filter (OSF) correction, as it affects bands outside of typical methane visibility (2100-2500nm). We also explore skipping bad pixel and ghost correction. We vectorise computations and merge repeated operations where possible. We highlight that the full on-the-ground pipeline strives for accurate science ready data products, meanwhile for fast on-board detection of very large methane leak events, some shortcuts can be taken. As a second optional step, we compute the matched filter product. We use a non-iterative spectrally wide variant. Finally, in the third step, we use a machine learning model either on the radiance data, or on the matched filter product computed for the same location. For end-to-end radiance data processing, we leverage models published in [3], namely the HyperEfficientViT (ConvUp) variant. For matched filter dependent models, we use models released in [6] using the U-Net architecture.

--- End source scope ---

Digital Twin Software simulates DENSO robots and equipment within a 3D virtual environment. It integrates the "realvirtual.io" software, which is designed for building digital twin spaces, with "Unity," the world's leading 3D development platform. It can help improve and optimize processes, such as verifying layouts without purchasing any actual equipment, training workers, and reducing setup adjustment time.

[a3:v1000000:r1000023:block:1001494:1:0]

[a3:v1000020:r1000086:block:1003767:1:0]
Realvirtual.io Professional is a Unity add-on that simplifies the creation of equipment design simulations. With its extensive library of assets, including conveyors and motors, you can intuitively build digital twin environments. It also enables easy simulation of equipment with support for TwinCAT and OPC UA interfaces, PLC connections, and software wiring.

[a3:v1000022:r1000105:block:1003856:1:0]
Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation > Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation > I. INTRODUCTION
Aerial manipulation is gaining popularity due to its ability to operate freely in 3D space, particularly in high-altitude environments that are difficult for humans to access [2]–[4]. Although fully autonomous manipulation remains the ultimate goal for robotics researchers, the complexity of the aerial environment necessitates keeping a human operator in the loop [5]. In our previous work [1], we proposed a six-degree-of-freedom teleoperation framework for aerial manipulation. Specifically, we designed four interaction modes for different tasks, including Spherical Mode and Cartesian Mode for long-range movement, Operation Mode for precise manipulation, and Locking Mode for temporary pauses, where hand gestures were utilized for seamless mode switching. The proposed framework was evaluated through a valve-turning task1, and to the best of our knowledge, this was the first time the rotational dexterity of the human wrist was intuitively demonstrated on an omnidirectional aerial robot. However, due to the limitations of both the controller and the physical structure of human forearm, we were not able to achieve continuous rotation.

Towards Robust Prehensile Manipulation in Open-Ended Environments > Towards Robust Prehensile Manipulation in Open-Ended Environments > 1. INTRODUCTION TO PREHENSILE MANIPULATION
Developing algorithms enabling robot prehensile manipulation tasks in dynamic real-world environments remains a major challenge in robotics. The manipulation problem aims at finding a set of suitable robot controls to change the state of an object from an initial to a desired configuration. More specifically, prehensile manipulation involves keeping the object grasped while the whole robot executes the manipulation using its control system [1]. For example opening a fridge is prehensile manipulating switching the object state from closed to open by grasping the fridge hammer during the whole robot motion. Solving robotic prehensile manipulation problems is inherently difficult due to the sparse nature of the grasping problem. In such scenarios, the space of solutions is extremely large, yet successful feedback is rare, making learning-based approaches particularly challenging. Moreover, the environments in which robots operate are highly variable—each static scene can differ significantly in object positions, shapes, levels of clutter, and semantic context [2]. For these reasons, prehensile manipulation is often described as an open-world or open-ended problem.

Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation > Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation > I. INTRODUCTION
Aerial manipulation is gaining popularity due to its ability to operate freely in 3D space, particularly in high-altitude environments that are difficult for humans to access [2]–[4]. Although fully autonomous manipulation remains the ultimate goal for robotics researchers, the complexity of the aerial environment necessitates keeping a human operator in the loop [5]. In our previous work [1], we proposed a six-degree-of-freedom teleoperation framework for aerial manipulation. Specifically, we designed four interaction modes for different tasks, including Spherical Mode and Cartesian Mode for long-range movement, Operation Mode for precise manipulation, and Locking Mode for temporary pauses, where hand gestures were utilized for seamless mode switching. The proposed framework was evaluated through a valve-turning task1, and to the best of our knowledge, this was the first time the rotational dexterity of the human wrist was intuitively demonstrated on an omnidirectional aerial robot. However, due to the limitations of both the controller and the physical structure of human forearm, we were not able to achieve continuous rotation.

Imaging Spectroscopy data consists of many spectrally narrow bands, sensors considered in this work span between 380 to 2500nm. As such, they offer visibility of a number of trace gases, nonetheless robust detection of these events remains challenging. The work of [3] first proposes the approach of using ML models for on-board detection of methane leak events. It defines two ways of processing data, either using end-to-end ML models which process radiance data directly, or via dependence on MF products. The work of [4] follows up in the direction of speeding up MF computations and then using ML models to reduce the number of false alarms.

[a3:v1000188:r1000277:block:1011699:1:0]
We present initial results from the deployment of machine learning models on-board of aerial platform used in the Tokyo-FC campaign. We present what we believe to be the first automated detection of methane leak on-board with machine learning, a significant and logical next step to the work of [1]. Predictions of our model, alongside with the collected data are available in the public portal at3. As future research, we aim to explore the usage of machine learning models recently proposed in [2] for multi-species detection of trace gases.

We start with the full EMIT on-the-ground pipeline described in [5]. First, we skip several steps in order to speed up the processing, while observing minimal differences in the computed products. In all cases, we avoid the order sorting filter (OSF) correction, as it affects bands outside of typical methane visibility (2100-2500nm). We also explore skipping bad pixel and ghost correction. We vectorise computations and merge repeated operations where possible. We highlight that the full on-the-ground pipeline strives for accurate science ready data products, meanwhile for fast on-board detection of very large methane leak events, some shortcuts can be taken. As a second optional step, we compute the matched filter product. We use a non-iterative spectrally wide variant. Finally, in the third step, we use a machine learning model either on the radiance data, or on the matched filter product computed for the same location. For end-to-end radiance data processing, we leverage models published in [3], namely the HyperEfficientViT (ConvUp) variant. For matched filter dependent models, we use models released in [6] using the U-Net architecture.
